::: {.why}
The calculation you did last night is the one that decides your data budget for the next decade, and it depends on your capital rather than on how good the data is.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Compute the break-even information ratio improvement that would justify a given data cost at a given account size.
- Name the two datasets that would most improve your own research, and say whether either is worth buying.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Do the arithmetic properly: a dataset costing a fixed amount a year, at a portfolio size and a volatility target, requires a specific improvement in annual return to pay for itself, which translates into a required improvement in information ratio. Tabulate it across three account sizes and note where the answer flips.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Apply it to your own case: rank the data you do not have by expected value, which for you is probably survivorship-free equity history first, then point-in-time analyst estimates, then intraday. Then check the free or institutional route for each, since WRDS and the open factor datasets cover more of the first two than most people realise.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the conclusion into the milestone: what you use, what you would buy at what size, and what you would never buy.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A break-even table for data cost against account size, and a ranked list of the datasets that would most improve your research.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
At your realistic account size, what annual data spend can you justify, and what would you spend it on first?
:::
